newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress -- frustrated and feisty.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress -- frustrated and feisty.

text.p: Clever ploy? Or desperate gamble?
India's Congress party has unleashed a political storm that analysts say could as easily engulf the nation's oldest party as hurl it back to power.

The whirlwind did not appear to be blowing in Congress's favour three days after its piqued president, Sitaram Kesri, threw down the gauntlet before his erstwhile ally, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
"Does the party with such a glorious past realise that it is fast becoming an endangered species in political terms?" The Asian Age newspaper said in an editorial.

Deve Gowda's United Front coalition -- a motley alliance of regional and national parties -- was standing firm behind the prime minister, who was unexpectedly thrust into power last June without any experience on the national stage.

The coalition, whose 15 parties control 180 votes in the 545-member lower house of parliament, has been propped up by Congress, which emerged from general elections last year with 140 seats -- its worst showing ever.
Waiting gleefully in the wings is the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the largest one with 162 deputies and confident that snap polls would propel it into power.

Why would Congress president Sitaram Kesri try to topple the government when his party is woefully short of a parliamentary majority and, according to opinion polls, would probably lose ground in mid-term elections?
"To me, this appears to be a desperate attempt which was unwarranted," Deve Gowda said on Tuesday.

In a letter to President Shankar Dayal Sharma on Sunday, Kesri cited a "deteriorating law and order situation, drift in the economy leading to rising prices and unemployment, growing communal menace and lack of cohesive functioning of the government".
But analysts said the letter obscured other reasons. Kesri appeared frustrated on the sidelines of power and perturbed by criminal investigations into himself and his allies.

Joined in the federal parliament by their shared fear of the BJP, Congress and the United Front have been increasingly at odds in crucial states, including Punjab and Uttar Pradesh where the BJP has formed coalition governments.
Kesri had hoped Congress would benefit from the United Front's support at the state level in exchange for its pivotal backing in New Delhi.
The Times of India said Kesri was convinced "the Gowda regime was following a game plan of wiping out the top echelon of the Congress party by involving them in criminal cases".
As the Indian Express said in a headline: "Kesri trying to save his skin".
Kesri, who took over the party in September when scandal-tainted former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao quit, has been linked to two investigations.
Other Congress leaders, some close to the party chief, others estranged, have also been targeted.
"The Congress leadership is unwilling to buy the argument that all the action against them is an instance of the law taking its own course," The Times of India said.
Kesri was pinning his hopes on splitting the United Front and joining forces with rebel parties including communists.

But he appeared to be coming around to the view that he might have to settle for less. "I am not against any member of the Steering Committee (of the United Front). My only complaint is against Deve Gowda," he said on Tuesday.

Newspapers said the political crisis could end in a myriad of ways. Congress could backtrack and renew its support for the United Front, either under Deve Gowda or a new leader, obviating the need for a trust vote on April 11.
G.K. Moopanar, head of the regional Tamil Maanila Congress party, has been cited as a possible United Front replacement for Deve Gowda -- although perhaps only in some months' time.
Congress could split or the BJP could abstain on April 11, giving Deve Gowda the necessary simple majority. Kesri accused Deve Gowda of trying to woo the BJP.
One of the more exotic possibilities had Deve Gowda being made vice president while the United Front backed Congress.
